findings.title: Providers with equal order are silently resolved by ServiceLoader order instead of failing
findings.body: The old code threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. The new code sorts by order() and silently takes the first one. When two providers share the same order, the winner depends on classpath/ServiceLoader iteration order and nothing is reported. Several existing modules declare order 200 (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider), so for example a FIPS build with the default provider also on the classpath would pick an arbitrary one. This silently changes the crypto backend, which is a security-relevant decision. Ties should still be rejected, or resolved by an explicit rule.

findings.title: New abstract method order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: order() is added as an abstract method on a public SPI interface. Any external or test implementation of CryptoProvider that is not updated will fail to compile. Since this is a new capability, a default implementation (for example returning 0 or some documented default) would avoid breaking implementors.

findings.title: Provider is auto-selected for third-party clients but throws for almost every operation
findings.body: AuthzClient.create() now calls CryptoIntegration.init(), which picks the highest-order provider on the classpath. For a third-party application that only has keycloak-authz-client, AuthzClientCryptoProvider (order 100) becomes the active provider. Most of its methods (getKeyFactory, getKeyPairGen, getSignature, getPemUtils, getCertificateUtils, getIdentityExtractorProvider, getAesGcmCipher, etc.) throw UnsupportedOperationException. Any code path in keycloak-core that calls CryptoIntegration.getProvider() for these, such as parsing PEM keys or RSA keys for client authentication, will fail with a confusing error rather than working. The exposure should be limited, or the unsupported methods should fail clearly and be documented.

findings.title: Dead ASN1 encoding computed and discarded in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 build two ASN1Encoder instances and throw away the results. The actual return value is computed separately at lines 117-121. The dead calls do unnecessary work and suggest the code was not reviewed carefully.

findings.title: Oversized integers in DER signatures are silently truncated
findings.body: integerToBytes() truncates to the last qLength bytes when the BigInteger is longer than the curve size. A malformed or malicious DER signature with an oversized r or s is therefore converted into a different, wrong concatenated signature instead of being rejected. The later verification will fail in a confusing way, or in the worst case the truncated value could be accepted by a verifier. The value should be range-checked and rejected.

findings.title: Test only checks round-trip consistency, not correctness against the JDK
findings.body: The test converts a JDK-produced DER signature to concatenated R||S and back, then compares the two concatenated forms. It never checks the output against the JDK's own verifier or a known vector, and it does not test the reverse direction starting from concatenated values with a specific length. A symmetric bug in both directions (for example a wrong byte-padding rule) would still pass. Verifying the signature with the JDK after conversion, and testing leading-zero and short-integer cases, would make the test meaningful.
